---
title: "Defensive Transcription on the Desk and on the Cluster: What a Local, Privacy-Conscious Speech-to-Text Workflow Can Be Shown to Do"
author:
  - name: Pablo Bernabeu
    affiliation: Department of Education, University of Oxford
    email: pablo.bernabeu@education.ox.ac.uk
abstract: |
  Automatic speech recognition is widely used for spoken data,
  yet cloud services sit awkwardly with the confidentiality
  obligations governing research recordings. This paper describes a workflow
  running Whisper Large v3 locally, on a laptop or institutional
  cluster, behind a layer of defensive post-processing
  meant to absorb the recogniser's errors, and that layer is measured
  instead of asserted. On clean English, the layer first cost
  0.40 percentage points of word error rate, 95% confidence interval [0.33, 0.48].
  Scoring each stage separately showed why: a contraction repair was
  rewriting ordinary English words, damaging 228 utterances and
  improving none. It reached users, and no design review or test
  caught it. Repaired, with further corrections and with all five
  corpora decoded again and scored under 17 conditions, the
  layer and the repaired stage cost nothing. Word error rate cannot
  test the property the layer is offered on. On the AMI Meeting Corpus,
  the layer preserves every filler the recogniser emits, though that is
  about a fifth of those a transcriber recorded. English-specific
  post-processing inflated error on six other languages up to eightfold
  until two further defects were repaired. Measured diarisation error
  depends more on how the corpus is reconstructed than on hyperparameter
  tuning. Default name masking redacts a name only if it is
  title-cased and already known, and a McAdams voice transformation
  brings linkage near chance only by destroying the transcript. As
  scored, quotation marks included, error rates differ 12-fold across
  40 readers of one clean corpus, a dispersion to plan around.
keywords: [speech recognition, Whisper, speaker diarisation, de-identification, reproducibility, research software]

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# An inherited C.UTF-8 locale is invalid on Windows R and falls back to C.
# format() then writes a minus sign as the literal text <U+2212> in table
# cells. Establish a UTF-8 character locale before any value is formatted;
# the numeric and collation locales are deliberately left alone.
if (!isTRUE(l10n_info()[["UTF-8"]])) {
  render_locale <- suppressWarnings(Sys.setlocale(
    "LC_CTYPE", if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") ".UTF-8" else "C.UTF-8"))
  if (!nzchar(render_locale) || !isTRUE(l10n_info()[["UTF-8"]]))
    stop("The manuscript requires a UTF-8 character locale. On Windows, ",
         "use R 4.2 or later; elsewhere make C.UTF-8 available.", call. = FALSE)
}

# The PDF's figures are drawn with cairo_pdf. The default pdf() device
# draws every ASCII hyphen with the minus glyph (its encodings map 0x2D to
# /minus), so axis titles such as "macro-averaged" and "Segment-end"
# printed with a minus sign in place of the hyphen. cairo_pdf draws a
# hyphen as a hyphen and U+2212 as a minus, and embeds its fonts. The
# HTML's figures are bitmaps and unaffected. An R built without cairo
# cannot open cairo_pdf, and there the figures fall back to pdf(), with
# its minus signs for hyphens, so that the render does not stop.
if (knitr::is_latex_output())
  knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = if (isTRUE(capabilities("cairo"))) "cairo_pdf"
                              else "pdf")

# Read one artefact by its extension. The tryCatch re-raises with the path
# attached; it never substitutes a value. A CSV that readr could only
# partly parse is refused as well, because a truncated or re-typed file
# otherwise yields a plausible but shorter table.
load_artefact <- function(path) {
  if (!file.exists(path))
    stop("Required artefact is missing: ", path, call. = FALSE)
  ext <- tolower(tools::file_ext(path))
  out <- tryCatch(
    switch(ext,
      json = jsonlite::fromJSON(path, simplifyVector = TRUE),
      csv  = readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE, progress = FALSE),
      cff  = yaml::read_yaml(path),
      readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")),
    error = function(e) stop("Required artefact could not be read: ", path,
                             ": ", conditionMessage(e), call. = FALSE))
  if (is.data.frame(out)) {
    if (nrow(out) == 0)
      stop("Required artefact has no rows: ", path, call. = FALSE)
    if (nrow(readr::problems(out)) > 0)
      stop("Required artefact did not parse cleanly: ", path, call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (length(out) == 0)
    stop("Required artefact is empty: ", path, call. = FALSE)
  out
}
artefacts <- c(
  lapply(manifest, \(rel) load_artefact(file.path(eval_dir, rel))),
  lapply(manifest_other, load_artefact)
)
list2env(artefacts, envir = environment())

has_field <- function(x, path) {
  for (key in strsplit(path, "/", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]) {
    if (is.null(x) || !(key %in% names(x))) return(FALSE)
    x <- x[[key]]
  }
  !is.null(x) && length(x) > 0 && !all(is.na(x))
}
for (name in names(required_fields)) {
  absent <- Filter(\(f) !has_field(artefacts[[name]], f),
                   required_fields[[name]])
  if (length(absent) > 0)
    stop("Artefact '", name, "' lacks the field(s) the text quotes: ",
         paste(absent, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Strict accessors and formatters
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A lookup that finds no row, or several, is an error: an inline number
# that silently became NA used to print as the letters "NA".
one <- function(x, what = deparse(substitute(x))) {
  if (length(x) != 1 || is.na(x))
    stop("Expected exactly one value for ", what, ", found ",
         length(x), call. = FALSE)
  x
}
f2  <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", one(x))
f3  <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", one(x))
ppt <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", 100 * one(x))   # proportion, as pp
pct <- function(x, accuracy = 0.1) scales::percent(one(x), accuracy = accuracy)
pc0 <- function(x) pct(x, accuracy = 1)
big <- function(x) format(one(x), big.mark = ",")
# A negative figure takes a true minus sign (U+2212), not a hyphen, as
# APA 7 asks; vectorised, for table columns as well as inline figures.
minus <- function(s) sub("^-", "\u2212", s)
# A signed difference in percentage points, as the prose and the tables
# of paired intervals print it.
sgn2 <- function(x) minus(sprintf("%+.2f", x))
# A correlation, which cannot exceed 1 in absolute value, printed as APA 7
# asks: two decimals, no leading zero, and a true minus sign.
r_apa <- function(x) minus(sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", sprintf("%.2f", one(x))))

# Words are retained at sentence openings. Elsewhere APA uses numerals
# from 10 upward; exact sample sizes are formatted with big() directly.
spell_count <- function(n) {
  n <- one(n)
  stopifnot(n == round(n), n >= 0)
  n <- as.integer(n)
  if (n >= 1000) return(format(n, big.mark = ","))
  ones <- c("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven",
            "eight", "nine", "ten", "eleven", "twelve", "thirteen",
            "fourteen", "fifteen", "sixteen", "seventeen", "eighteen",
            "nineteen")
  tens <- c("", "", "twenty", "thirty", "forty", "fifty", "sixty",
            "seventy", "eighty", "ninety")
  if (n < 20) return(ones[[n + 1]])
  if (n < 100) {
    r <- n %% 10
    return(if (r == 0) tens[[n %/% 10 + 1]]
           else paste0(tens[[n %/% 10 + 1]], "-", ones[[r + 1]]))
  }
  h <- paste(ones[[n %/% 100 + 1]], "hundred")
  if (n %% 100 == 0) h else paste(h, "and", spell_count(n %% 100))
}
num_word <- function(n) {
  if (one(n) >= 10) big(n) else spell_count(n)
}
Num_word <- function(n) {
  w <- spell_count(n)
  paste0(toupper(substring(w, 1, 1)), substring(w, 2))
}
# "a, b and c" from a character vector.
and_list <- function(x) {
  stopifnot(length(x) >= 1)
  if (length(x) == 1) x else
    paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}

# Single accessor for the model-by-corpus-by-condition grid, so that
# every figure quoted from it in the Results reads the same artefact.
mw <- function(model, suite, cond) {
  one(sweep_agg$macro_wer[sweep_agg$model_slug == model &
                          sweep_agg$suite == suite &
                          sweep_agg$condition == cond],
      paste("macro WER of", model, suite, cond))
}

# Utterance counts per corpus, read from the same grid, so that the
# corpus descriptions in the Methods cannot drift from the runs they
# describe. The raw condition is the one every suite carries at full
# length; `whisper_norm` drops empty references and so scores fewer.
n_utt <- function(suite, cond = "raw", model = "whisper-large-v3") {
  as.integer(one(sweep_agg$n_utterances[sweep_agg$model_slug == model &
                                        sweep_agg$suite == suite &
                                        sweep_agg$condition == cond],
                 paste("utterances of", model, suite, cond)))
}
n_utt_txt <- function(suite, ...) big(n_utt(suite, ...))

# The code the reported sweep ran, as the aggregate records it. One
# grid, one version: a grid mixing runs of different code is refused.
sweep_version <- unique(sweep_agg$pipeline_version)
if (length(sweep_version) != 1)
  stop("sweep_aggregate.csv mixes pipeline versions: ",
       paste(sweep_version, collapse = "; "), call. = FALSE)
n_sweep_conditions <- length(unique(sweep_agg$condition))
n_sweep_suites     <- length(unique(sweep_agg$suite))
n_sweep_models     <- length(unique(sweep_agg$model_slug))

# The headline files are one cell of that grid: the summary is the
# sweep's raw Large v3 test-clean summary, the report is post_raw, the
# baseline of the paired intervals, and the interval was drawn on that
# report. Until the re-run they held an earlier decode than the grid
# (audit findings MS-12, OUTPUTS-03), so each is tied to it here. The
# tolerance on the grid's cell absorbs the last binary digit, which
# readr and jsonlite can parse differently from the same decimal. The
# interval counts as drawn on the report when it covers as many
# utterances and its mean is the report's to the six decimals it keeps.
local({
  checks <- c(
    "the summary was written by the sweep's code" =
      startsWith(wer_summary$run_metadata$git_commit, sweep_version),
    "the summary is the grid's raw Large v3 test-clean cell" =
      abs(wer_summary$summary$macro_wer -
            mw("whisper-large-v3", "librispeech_clean", "raw")) < 1e-12,
    "wer_report.csv is post_raw" =
      identical(names(wer_report), names(post_raw)) &&
      all(vapply(names(wer_report),
                 \(k) identical(wer_report[[k]], post_raw[[k]]),
                 logical(1))),
    "wer_ci.csv was drawn on wer_report.csv" =
      nrow(wer_ci) == 1 && wer_ci$n == nrow(wer_report) &&
      abs(wer_ci$macro_wer - mean(wer_report$wer)) < 5e-7)
  if (!all(checks))
    stop("The headline files are not the condition sweep's raw Large v3 ",
         "test-clean cell and its interval; failed: ",
         paste(names(checks)[!checks], collapse = "; "), call. = FALSE)
})

# Decode precision as the prose names it, from the dtype a run recorded
# ("torch.float16" or "float16"). The WER benchmark passes the pipeline
# no dtype on a GPU, so transformers loads the precision each checkpoint
# stores and the sweep's models did not all decode alike. Of the sweep's
# summaries only the headline cell's is committed, so Large v3's is the
# one read here; the timestamp benchmark records its own.
precision_word <- function(dtype) {
  words <- c(float16 = "half precision", float32 = "single precision")
  key <- sub("^torch\\.", "", one(dtype))
  if (!key %in% names(words))
    stop("No wording for the decode precision ", dtype, call. = FALSE)
  words[[key]]
}
wer_precision <- precision_word(wer_summary$benchmark$decode$dtype)
ts_precision  <- precision_word(ts_summary$whisper$dtype)

# Per-language counts for the multilingual wave, used by the Methods well
# before the Results chunk reads the same artefact for its rates.
ml_utt <- function(split) {
  big(as.integer(one(ml$languages[[split]]$utterances,
                     paste("FLEURS utterances for", split))))
}
# The cards the last multilingual pass ran on, which its summary records
# language by language, each named once and without the vendor's name,
# which the Methods print before the list.
ml_last_cards <- local({
  arms <- ml$benchmark$arms
  gpus <- unlist(arms[[length(arms)]][["gpus"]])
  if (length(gpus) == 0)
    stop("fleurs_multilingual_summary.json: the last arm names no card",
         call. = FALSE)
  unique(sub("^NVIDIA ", "", gpus))
})

# Bootstrap settings, read from the artefacts instead of asserted in the
# prose that quotes them. A percentile bound is itself an estimate and
# carries Monte Carlo error, so the bounds move in the fourth decimal
# with the replicate count and the seed, and a bound lying near a
# rounding threshold can print either way. The Methods quote one count
# for every interval in the paper, so the interval artefacts must
# agree, and within each the count must be a single value (audit
# findings MS-16, REGEN-03). The caption of @tbl-condition-ci reads its
# own artefact's count in load-condition-ci.
boot_counts <- list(wer_ci = unique(wer_ci$bootstrap),
                    condition_ci_postfix = unique(cci$bootstrap),
                    condition_ci = unique(cci_pre$bootstrap),
                    speaker_cluster = unique(c(sc_ci$macro_wer$bootstrap,
                                               sc_ci$paired_deltas$bootstrap)))
if (any(lengths(boot_counts) != 1) ||
    length(unique(unlist(boot_counts))) != 1)
  stop("The interval artefacts do not share one bootstrap replicate ",
       "count, so the Methods cannot quote one: ",
       paste(names(boot_counts), vapply(boot_counts, toString, ""),
             sep = " = ", collapse = "; "), call. = FALSE)
boot_b     <- as.integer(boot_counts$wer_ci)
boot_b_txt <- big(boot_b)
boot_seeds <- unique(c(wer_ci$seed, cci$seed, cci_pre$seed,
                       sc_ci$macro_wer$seed, sc_ci$paired_deltas$seed))
stopifnot(length(boot_seeds) == 1)

# The sensitivity must describe these reports and preserve their macro
# estimand. Reader labels come from LibriSpeech's utterance identifiers;
# each cluster contributes its WER sum and its utterance count. The
# paired point estimates are recomputed from matched utterances, tying
# counts and means to the reports. The regeneration gate independently
# rebuilds the intervals to check their freshness.
sc_level <- sc_ci$macro_wer
sc_paired <- sc_ci$paired_deltas
sc_conditions <- sub("^wer_report_(.*)\\.csv$", "\\1",
                     basename(sc_paired$condition$path))
stopifnot(sc_ci$schema_version == 1,
          sc_ci$resampling_unit == "LibriSpeech reader",
          sc_ci$estimand == paste0("mean per-utterance WER; paired deltas ",
                                  "are condition minus baseline"),
          nrow(sc_paired) == 2,
          setequal(sc_conditions, c("contraction_fix", "pipeline_full")))
sc_pair <- function(condition) {
  hit <- which(sc_conditions == condition)
  if (length(hit) != 1)
    stop("Speaker-cluster sensitivity lacks a unique condition: ",
         condition, call. = FALSE)
  sc_paired[hit, , drop = FALSE]
}
check_sc_point <- function(cell, report, baseline = NULL) {
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(report$name),
            all(grepl("^[0-9]+-[0-9]+-[0-9]+$", report$name)),
            cell$n_utterances == nrow(report),
            cell$n_readers == length(unique(sub("-.*$", "", report$name))))
  values <- report$wer
  if (!is.null(baseline)) {
    stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(baseline$name),
              setequal(report$name, baseline$name))
    values <- values - baseline$wer[match(report$name, baseline$name)]
  }
  stopifnot(abs(cell$estimate - mean(values)) < 1e-12,
            is.finite(cell$ci_lo), is.finite(cell$ci_hi),
            cell$ci_lo <= cell$estimate, cell$estimate <= cell$ci_hi)
}
check_sc_point(sc_level, wer_report)
check_sc_point(sc_pair("contraction_fix"), pre_contraction, pre_raw)
check_sc_point(sc_pair("pipeline_full"), pre_composite, pre_raw)
stopifnot(basename(sc_level$source$path) == "wer_report.csv",
          all(basename(sc_paired$baseline$path) == "wer_report.csv"),
          all(sc_paired$n_utterances == sc_level$n_utterances),
          all(sc_paired$n_readers == sc_level$n_readers))

# The alternative scoring report must retain the original matrix and
# compare the same scored utterances across rules. Its point estimates
# are checked against both the canonical aggregate and its separate CSV.
# Exact per-utterance verification belongs to the producer and gate,
# because the recovered hypothesis bundle is not a render dependency.
ss_cells <- scorer_sens$cells
ss_keys <- paste(ss_cells$suite, ss_cells$model_slug, sep = "/")
ss_expected <- sweep_agg[sweep_agg$condition == "raw", ]
stopifnot(scorer_sens$schema_version == 1,
          scorer_sens$provenance$original_scoring_verified,
          identical(scorer_sens$transform$after,
                    "evaluation.wer.normalise_text(..., strip_header=False)"),
          identical(scorer_sens$transform$pattern, "(?<!\\w)'|'(?!\\w)"),
          identical(scorer_sens$transform$replacement, " "),
          identical(scorer_sens$transform$whitespace, "collapse and strip"),
          setequal(scorer_sens$transform$sides, c("reference", "hypothesis")),
          !anyDuplicated(ss_keys),
          setequal(ss_keys, paste(ss_expected$suite,
                                 ss_expected$model_slug, sep = "/")),
          all(c("newly_excluded_shared_uids", "newly_included_shared_uids") %in%
                names(ss_cells$cross_rule_sample)),
          all(lengths(ss_cells$cross_rule_sample$newly_excluded_shared_uids) == 0),
          all(lengths(ss_cells$cross_rule_sample$newly_included_shared_uids) == 0),
          nrow(scorer_sens_table) == nrow(ss_cells) * 4)
ss_csv_keys <- with(scorer_sens_table,
  paste(suite, model_slug, condition, scoring_rule, sep = "/"))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(ss_csv_keys))
for (condition in c("raw", "whisper_norm")) {
  detail <- ss_cells$conditions[[condition]]
  canonical <- sweep_agg[sweep_agg$condition == condition, ]
  canonical <- canonical[match(ss_keys, paste(canonical$suite,
    canonical$model_slug, sep = "/")), ]
  stopifnot(!anyNA(canonical$suite),
            all(detail$original_per_utterance_and_aggregate_verified),
            all(detail$n_newly_excluded == 0),
            all(detail$n_newly_included == 0),
            all(detail$original$files == canonical$n_utterances),
            all(detail$edge_apostrophe$files == detail$original$files),
            all(abs(detail$original$macro_wer - canonical$macro_wer) < 1e-12),
            all(abs(detail$original$micro_wer - canonical$micro_wer) < 1e-12))
  for (rule in c("original", "edge_apostrophe")) {
    values <- detail[[rule]]
    matched <- scorer_sens_table[match(paste(ss_keys, condition, rule,
      sep = "/"), ss_csv_keys), ]
    stopifnot(!anyNA(matched$suite),
              all(is.finite(values$macro_wer)),
              all(is.finite(values$micro_wer)),
              all(values$macro_wer >= 0), all(values$micro_wer >= 0),
              all(values$files == matched$n_scored),
              all(abs(values$macro_wer - matched$macro_wer) < 1e-12),
              all(abs(values$micro_wer - matched$micro_wer) < 1e-12))
    shared <- ss_cells$paired_gains_on_fixed_cross_rule_sample[[rule]]
    stopifnot(all(shared$n_shared == ss_cells$cross_rule_sample$n_common),
              all(shared$n_shared == ss_cells$conditions$whisper_norm$original$files),
              all(abs(shared$macro_gain_shared -
                (shared$macro_baseline_shared - shared$macro_condition_shared) /
                 shared$macro_baseline_shared) < 1e-12))
    if (condition == "whisper_norm")
      stopifnot(all(abs(shared$macro_gain_shared -
                        matched$macro_gain_shared) < 1e-12))
  }
}
ss_gain <- function(suite, model, rule) {
  hit <- which(ss_cells$suite == suite & ss_cells$model_slug == model)
  one(ss_cells$paired_gains_on_fixed_cross_rule_sample[[rule]]$
        macro_gain_shared[hit], paste("scorer sensitivity", suite, model, rule))
}
ss_gain_txt <- function(suite, model, rule)
  pct(ss_gain(suite, model, rule))
# The module default the Methods contrast it with, read from the module.
py_constant <- function(lines, name) {
  hit <- grep(paste0("^", name, "\\s*=\\s*[0-9_]+\\s*(#.*)?$"), lines,
              value = TRUE)
  if (length(hit) != 1)
    stop("Cannot read ", name, " from its module", call. = FALSE)
  as.integer(gsub("_", "", sub("^[^=]*=\\s*([0-9_]+).*$", "\\1", hit)))
}
boot_default <- py_constant(bootstrap_py, "_DEFAULT_BOOTSTRAP")

# Dependency floors and the locked versions of the cluster environment,
# read from the files the Methods describe.
req_floor <- function(pkg) {
  hit <- trimws(req_lines)
  hit <- hit[startsWith(hit, paste0(pkg, ">="))]
  if (length(hit) != 1)
    stop("requirements.txt has no single floor for ", pkg, call. = FALSE)
  sub(",.*$", "", substring(hit, nchar(pkg) + 3))
}
lock_version <- function(pkg) {
  hit <- trimws(lock_lines)
  hit <- hit[startsWith(hit, paste0(pkg, "=="))]
  if (length(hit) != 1)
    stop("requirements-lock.txt has no single pin for ", pkg, call. = FALSE)
  substring(hit, nchar(pkg) + 3)
}
# A date as the prose writes it, "26 September 2026", in any locale.
long_date <- function(d) {
  d <- as.Date(one(d))
  paste(as.integer(format(d, "%d")), month.name[as.integer(format(d, "%m"))],
        format(d, "%Y"))
}
# When the lock was taken, from its header. The audit's re-runs on the
# cluster, made after it, record the package versions they imported
# (run_metadata, or `run` in the timestamp summary), and off_lock()
# names those that differ from the lock or that it does not pin;
# character(0) means the record matches. Names are compared as pip
# compares them (PEP 503), so that a record's `huggingface_hub` finds
# the lock's `huggingface-hub`, and a package recorded as absent (null)
# is not compared.
lock_taken <- local({
  hit <- regmatches(lock_lines, regexpr("Taken on [0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}",
                                        lock_lines))
  if (length(hit) != 1)
    stop("requirements-lock.txt does not say once when it was taken",
         call. = FALSE)
  as.Date(sub("Taken on ", "", hit, fixed = TRUE))
})
lock_taken_txt <- long_date(lock_taken)
pep503 <- function(x) gsub("[-_.]+", "-", tolower(x))
lock_pins <- local({
  pins <- trimws(lock_lines)
  pins <- pins[grepl("^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*==", pins)]
  stats::setNames(sub("^[^=]+==", "", pins), pep503(sub("==.*$", "", pins)))
})
if (length(lock_pins) == 0 || anyDuplicated(names(lock_pins)))
  stop("requirements-lock.txt does not pin each package once", call. = FALSE)
off_lock <- function(packages) {
  have <- unlist(packages)
  if (length(have) == 0)
    stop("A run's record lists no package versions", call. = FALSE)
  pinned <- unname(lock_pins[pep503(names(have))])
  names(have)[is.na(pinned) | pinned != unname(have)]
}
wer_off_lock  <- off_lock(wer_summary$run_metadata$packages)
anon_off_lock <- off_lock(anon$run_metadata$packages)
ts_off_lock   <- off_lock(ts_summary$run$packages)

# Filler-preservation results; the disfluency section precedes the
# diarisation chunk, so the accessor lives here. `conditions` holds each
# condition's own utterances, the whole AMI test split except where the
# canonical normaliser empties a reference and drops the utterance;
# dshared() reads the same figures over the utterances every condition
# scores, which are the normaliser's own set. The normaliser's count of
# what it dropped must close the gap between the two.
dcond <- function(name, field) {
  one(disfl$conditions[[name]][[field]],
      paste("disfluency", name, field))
}
dshared <- function(name, field) {
  one(disfl$conditions_shared_set[[name]][[field]],
      paste("disfluency, shared set,", name, field))
}
if (dshared("raw", "n_utterances") != dcond("whisper_norm", "n_utterances") ||
    dcond("whisper_norm", "n_utterances_dropped") !=
      dcond("raw", "n_utterances") - dcond("whisper_norm", "n_utterances"))
  stop("disfluency_summary.json: the shared set and the utterances the ",
       "normaliser dropped do not add up to the split", call. = FALSE)
# Reference recall of the model's own output inside the utterances the
# normaliser drops and over the rest: the transcriber's fillers the
# model emitted in each part, over those the transcriber recorded there.
disfl_recall_dropped <-
  (dcond("raw", "reference_recovered") -
     dshared("raw", "reference_recovered")) /
  (dcond("raw", "reference_fillers") - dshared("raw", "reference_fillers"))
disfl_recall_kept <- dshared("raw", "reference_recovered") /
  dshared("raw", "reference_fillers")

# The diarisation collar, which the Methods quote before the diarisation
# chunk runs. Every DER artefact must have been scored under the same
# one. It is pyannote.metrics' total width, centred on each reference
# boundary (audit finding EDER-01).
der_collar <- unique(c(der_summary$collar_s, der_tuned$collar_s,
                       der_oracle$collar_s, der_concat$collar_s,
                       der_sel$collar_s, der_sel2$collar_s))
if (length(der_collar) != 1)
  stop("The DER artefacts were scored under different collars: ",
       toString(der_collar), call. = FALSE)
der_dev_meetings <- unique(c(der_sweep$n_meetings, der_sweep2$n_meetings))
stopifnot(length(der_dev_meetings) == 1)
# The finer development grid's cells, which the Methods count; the second
# sweep scores them together with one row for the pipeline's defaults,
# which carries no setting of its own.
der_grid2_n <- sum(!is.na(der_sweep2$clustering_threshold))
stopifnot(nrow(der_sweep2) == der_grid2_n + 1,
          der_sel2$n_configurations == nrow(der_sweep2))
# The scan's points are counted from its setting rows in the same way. The
# committed scan, the October re-run (hpc/runs/der_sweep.env), scores the
# defaults too, as the August scan did not, so the scan may carry a
# defaults row or not, and the Methods say whether each sweep was scored
# beside the defaults.
der_scan_n <- sum(!is.na(der_sweep$clustering_threshold))
stopifnot((nrow(der_sweep) - der_scan_n) %in% c(0, 1),
          der_sel$n_configurations == nrow(der_sweep))
der_defaults_both <- nrow(der_sweep) > der_scan_n
# The code the diarisation runs ran, which every summary and both sweep
# selections record, from a clean tree; the Methods print it and compare
# the summaries' package versions with the lock (lock_matches in the
# claims check).
der_runs <- list(der_summary, der_tuned, der_oracle, der_concat)
der_commit <- unique(substr(c(
  vapply(der_runs, \(s) one(s$run_metadata$git_commit, "a DER run's commit"),
         character(1)),
  one(der_sel$git_commit), one(der_sel2$git_commit)), 1, 7))
stopifnot(length(der_commit) == 1,
          all(vapply(der_runs, \(s) identical(s$run_metadata$git_dirty, FALSE),
                     logical(1))),
          # the Methods name their cards from the run records, "because
          # the summaries do not": no field name or value names a device
          !any(vapply(der_runs, \(s) {
            u <- unlist(s)
            any(grepl("gpu|cuda|card|device|accelerator|nvidia|l40s",
                      c(names(u), as.character(u)), ignore.case = TRUE))
          }, logical(1))))

# Which AMI meetings and speakers the timestamp and anonymisation samples
# cover, and how many utterances each meeting gives (per_meeting), read
# from their per-utterance reports. AMI IHM utterance ids read
# AMI_<meeting>_<channel>_<speaker>_<begin>_<end>. The timestamp
# sample is the scored utterances together with the ones it could not
# score (timestamp_skipped.csv, which gives the reason and what the
# recogniser wrote for each), since the Methods describe all of them.
ami_ids <- function(ids) {
  parts <- strsplit(unique(ids), "_", fixed = TRUE)
  stopifnot(all(lengths(parts) >= 4),
            all(vapply(parts, `[`, "", 1) == "AMI"))
  meeting <- vapply(parts, `[`, "", 2)
  list(meetings = sort(unique(meeting)),
       speakers = sort(unique(vapply(parts, `[`, "", 4))),
       per_meeting = c(table(meeting)))
}
if (nrow(ts_skipped) != ts_summary$n_skipped ||
    any(ts_skipped$audio_id %in% ts_report$audio_id))
  stop("timestamp_skipped.csv does not list the utterances the summary ",
       "says were left unscored", call. = FALSE)
ts_ami   <- ami_ids(c(ts_report$audio_id, ts_skipped$audio_id))
anon_ami <- ami_ids(anon_report$uid)
ts_first <- as.integer(ts_summary$n + ts_summary$n_skipped)

# The anonymisation summary must describe the sample its report holds,
# meeting by meeting: the same meetings and speakers, and from each
# meeting as many utterances as the summary says it accepted there.
# anon_cap_met says whether every meeting gave the per-meeting cap, as
# the Methods say it did, so it rests on the report as well.
anon_accepted <- unlist(anon$accepted_by_meeting)
if (anon$n_meetings != length(anon_ami$meetings) ||
    !setequal(names(anon_accepted), anon_ami$meetings) ||
    any(anon_ami$per_meeting[names(anon_accepted)] != anon_accepted) ||
    sum(anon_accepted) != anon$n_utterances ||
    anon$n_speakers != length(anon_ami$speakers))
  stop("anonymisation_summary.json does not describe the sample in ",
       "anonymisation_report.csv", call. = FALSE)
anon_cap_met <- all(anon_accepted == anon$per_meeting_cap)
# The single-meeting run is the same benchmark on another sample, so a
# comparison of the two must not mix code, coefficients or models.
if (!identical(anon_single$git_commit, anon$git_commit) ||
    !identical(names(anon_single$by_alpha), names(anon$by_alpha)) ||
    !identical(anon_single$asr_model, anon$asr_model) ||
    !identical(anon_single$embedding_model, anon$embedding_model))
  stop("The single-meeting anonymisation run differs from the canonical ",
       "one in more than its sample", call. = FALSE)

# The determinism check: one seed run twice, then a second seed once, in
# each of its four runs, on an H100 (ARC job 8554985, the top-level
# files), an L40S (8781724), a V100 (8978760) and a processor alone
# (8978759), all over the same first utterances of the AMI test split.
# Their summaries give only how many they compared, so det_n checks that
# the counts agree. That they are the same utterances rests on the
# comparison below, which records that its runs list the same ids
# (meta/shared/corpus_source). det_own_agree says, run by run, whether
# the repeat and the second seed gave the first decode's words on every
# utterance. The names are the comparison's.
det_own <- list(
  h100       = list(rep = det_repeat,      seeds = det_seeds),
  l40s       = list(rep = det_l40s_repeat, seeds = det_l40s_seeds),
  v100_seed0 = list(rep = det_v100_repeat, seeds = det_v100_seeds),
  cpu        = list(rep = det_cpu_repeat,  seeds = det_cpu_seeds))
det_n <- unique(unlist(lapply(det_own, \(r) c(r$rep$utterances_compared,
                                              r$seeds$utterances_compared))))
det_seed_of <- function(run) sub("_run[0-9]+$", "", run)
stopifnot(length(det_n) == 1,
          all(vapply(det_own, \(r)
            length(r$rep$runs) == 2 &&
              length(unique(det_seed_of(r$rep$runs))) == 1 &&
              length(r$seeds$runs) == 2 &&
              length(unique(det_seed_of(r$seeds$runs))) == 2,
            logical(1))))
det_own_agree <- vapply(det_own, \(r) r$rep$identical == det_n &&
                          r$seeds$identical == det_n, logical(1))
# The card a job wrote into its gpu.txt, or the processor the CPU run
# wrote into its cpu.txt: the first non-empty line.
gpu_line <- function(lines) {
  lines <- trimws(lines)
  lines <- lines[nzchar(lines)]
  if (length(lines) == 0)
    stop("A gpu.txt or cpu.txt names no device", call. = FALSE)
  lines[[1]]
}
det_gpu_name <- sub("^NVIDIA ", "", gpu_line(det_gpu))
# The processor as the prose names it, without the core count.
det_cpu_name <- sub("\\s+[0-9]+-Core Processor$", "", gpu_line(det_cpu_proc))

# The same decode in several hardware configurations, as
# determinism_cross_accelerator.json records them: the check's four runs
# and the condition sweep's V100 decode of the same utterances (v100). A
# configuration is a card with the node that holds it, or a node's
# processor where no card was used; the sweep's decode and the check's
# V100 run (v100_seed0) share one. The runs also differ in seed, code
# version and process. The L40S, both V100 runs and the processor run
# kept their transcripts and are compared word for word (det_x is the
# L40S against the sweep, with the word edits of each utterance that
# differs in det_x_edits). The H100's transcripts were lost, and it
# enters through the per-utterance error rates its log printed, which can
# show a difference but never agreement, so det_h_l (against the L40S)
# and det_h_v (against the sweep) are lower bounds. det_pooled is each
# run's pooled WER over the subset, det_node, det_commit and det_date say
# where, at which code and when each ran, and det_card_all gives each
# run's card, NA for a run on a processor alone (det_cards keeps the
# cards, and det_card_names drops the vendor's name, as det_gpu_name
# does). All read every run the file lists, past what the field checks
# cover, so they match names exactly: `$` would also take a longer name
# that begins with the one asked for, such as the accelerator_source the
# file pairs with each accelerator. A run counts as one on a processor
# alone when its accelerator is absent, null or, as the file records a
# fact it lacks, a phrase opening "none" or "not recorded". Only a name
# opening NVIDIA, or Tesla or Quadro as the names of some older cards do,
# counts as a card, and any other accelerator stops the setup.
det_rn   <- names(det_cross$meta$runs)
det_meta <- function(run, key)
  one(det_cross$meta$runs[[run]][[key]], paste("determinism run", run, key))
det_node   <- vapply(det_rn, det_meta, character(1), key = "node")
det_commit <- vapply(det_rn, det_meta, character(1), key = "code_commit")
det_date   <- as.Date(vapply(det_rn, det_meta, character(1), key = "date"))
names(det_date) <- det_rn
det_x          <- det_cross$text$l40s_vs_v100
det_x_edits    <- as.integer(det_x$differing_utterances$word_edits)
det_h_l        <- det_cross$wer_level$h100_vs_l40s$wer_differs
det_h_v        <- det_cross$wer_level$h100_vs_v100$wer_differs
det_pooled     <- vapply(det_cross$subset_wer,
                         \(r) one(r[["micro_wer"]], "a run's pooled WER"),
                         numeric(1))
det_card_of    <- function(run) {
  a <- det_cross$meta$runs[[run]][["accelerator"]]
  if (is.null(a) ||
      (length(a) == 1 && (is.na(a) || grepl("^(none|not recorded)\\b", a,
                                             ignore.case = TRUE))))
    return(NA_character_)
  if (!is.character(a) || length(a) != 1 ||
      !grepl("^(NVIDIA|Tesla|Quadro)\\b", a))
    stop("determinism_cross_accelerator.json: run '", run, "' names an ",
         "accelerator that is neither a card nor marked as absent: ",
         toString(a), call. = FALSE)
  a
}
det_card_all   <- vapply(det_rn, det_card_of, character(1))
det_cards      <- det_card_all[!is.na(det_card_all)]
det_card_names <- sub("^NVIDIA ", "", det_cards)
# Runs, configurations and the cards of the check's own runs, as the
# Methods count them. The run on a processor alone is the CPU run.
det_proc_run   <- names(det_card_all)[is.na(det_card_all)]
det_config     <- paste(det_node,
                        ifelse(is.na(det_card_all), "processor", det_card_all))
det_n_runs        <- length(det_rn)
det_n_configs     <- length(unique(det_config))
det_n_gpu_configs <- length(unique(det_config[!is.na(det_card_all)]))
det_n_own_cards   <- sum(!is.na(det_card_all[names(det_own)]))
# The check's runs made before and after the lock was taken, which the
# Methods count apart (lock_taken is read from the lock above).
det_n_own_after_lock  <- sum(det_date[names(det_own)] > lock_taken)
det_n_own_before_lock <- length(det_own) - det_n_own_after_lock
# The precision of the decodes: the check's V100 run records the
# checkpoint's half precision, which the comparison gives every run on a
# GPU, and the processor run records the single precision it was asked
# for (meta/shared/precision).
det_precision     <- precision_word(det_meta("v100_seed0", "precision"))
det_cpu_precision <- precision_word(det_meta(det_proc_run, "precision"))
# The meeting the compared utterances come from, by their ids.
det_meetings <- ami_ids(det_l40s_report$name)$meetings
stopifnot(det_cross$subset$utterances == det_n,
          nrow(det_l40s_report) == det_n,
          det_cross$references$utterances_whose_reference_differs == 0,
          all(vapply(det_cross$text, \(p) p$utterances_compared == det_n,
                     logical(1))),
          length(det_x_edits) == det_x$differing,
          # the check's own runs and the sweep's decode, and no other
          setequal(det_rn, c(names(det_own), "v100")),
          setequal(names(det_cross$subset_wer), det_rn),
          # one run on a processor alone, the CPU run, and the GPU runs
          # in half precision, as the comparison says of all of them
          identical(det_proc_run, "cpu"),
          grepl(paste0("^float16 for the ", num_word(length(det_cards)),
                       " GPU runs"), det_cross$meta$shared$precision),
          det_precision != det_cpu_precision,
          # "all from meeting", one meeting
          length(det_meetings) == 1,
          # the comparison names the cards the jobs wrote into gpu.txt,
          # and the processor the CPU run wrote into cpu.txt
          det_cards[["h100"]] == gpu_line(det_gpu),
          det_cards[["l40s"]] == gpu_line(det_l40s_gpu),
          det_cards[["v100_seed0"]] == gpu_line(det_v100_gpu),
          startsWith(det_meta("cpu", "host_processor"), gpu_line(det_cpu_proc)))
# The Methods list the check's own runs in the order they were submitted:
# "ran first on" the H100, then "repeated on" the L40S, the processor and
# the V100 (the CPU and V100 runs share a date, so their job numbers
# order them).
det_job_no <- vapply(c("h100", "l40s", "cpu", "v100_seed0"), \(r)
  as.numeric(sub("^([0-9]+).*$", "\\1", det_meta(r, "job"))), numeric(1))
stopifnot(setequal(names(det_job_no), names(det_own)),
          !is.unsorted(det_job_no, strictly = TRUE))

# The scheduler ledger, which the Methods describe before the footprint
# section reads it. fp_jobs joins each job's allocation (the ledger) to
# its category and the board power it was priced at (the report the
# footprint module wrote from the ledger). The two list the same jobs,
# the summary counts them, and the summary and the ledger's provenance
# name the same capture and dump. A job holds one GPU or none, and the
# board is given exactly for the jobs that hold one.
fp_jobs <- merge(fp_ledger, fp_report, by = "job_id",
                 suffixes = c("", "_report"))
# "captured ... after the evaluation's last job had finished": the dump
# held no job of this project still pending or running (the field is
# present and empty).
stopifnot(!is.null(fp$provenance$left_out_unfinished),
          length(fp$provenance$left_out_unfinished) == 0,
          nrow(fp_jobs) == nrow(fp_ledger), nrow(fp_jobs) == nrow(fp_report),
          nrow(fp_jobs) == one(fp$overall$n_jobs),
          identical(fp_ledger_prov$sacct_sha256, fp$provenance$sacct_sha256),
          identical(fp_ledger_prov$captured, fp$provenance$captured),
          all(fp_jobs$gpus %in% c(0, 1)),
          identical(fp_jobs$gpus == 1, !is.na(fp_jobs$gpu_type)),
          identical(is.na(fp_jobs$gpu_type), is.na(fp_jobs$gpu_type_report)),
          all(fp_jobs$gpu_type == fp_jobs$gpu_type_report, na.rm = TRUE))
fp_gpu_jobs <- fp_jobs[fp_jobs$gpus == 1, ]
# "read from the node it ran on, the board of every GPU" (the builder maps
# each job's node to its board, provenance gpu_model_source, and the
# ledger keeps the board alone): each GPU job is priced at
# its board's power in the summary's parameters, and none carries the
# label of a family (a100, p100, v100 or h100), which covers boards of
# different power and would be priced at the family's largest.
fp_tdp_w <- unlist(fp$parameters$gpu_tdp_w)
stopifnot(all(fp_gpu_jobs$gpu_type %in% names(fp_tdp_w)),
          all(fp_gpu_jobs$tdp_w == fp_tdp_w[fp_gpu_jobs$gpu_type]),
          !any(fp_gpu_jobs$gpu_type %in% c("a100", "p100", "v100", "h100")),
          grepl("NodeList", one(fp_ledger_prov$gpu_model_source)))
fp_n_boards <- length(unique(fp_gpu_jobs$gpu_type))
# What the GPU jobs held, as the submission scripts request it: the
# range of cores and memory over every GPU job outside the probes, and
# the probes that held less, which the Methods set apart as diarisation
# probes. The determinism check's processor run held cores alone.
fp_probe_cat <- grepl("probe", fp_gpu_jobs$category, ignore.case = TRUE)
fp_cores <- range(fp_gpu_jobs$cpus[!fp_probe_cat])
fp_mem   <- range(fp_gpu_jobs$mem_gb[!fp_probe_cat])
fp_odd   <- fp_gpu_jobs[fp_gpu_jobs$cpus < fp_cores[[1]] |
                          fp_gpu_jobs$cpus > fp_cores[[2]] |
                          fp_gpu_jobs$mem_gb < fp_mem[[1]] |
                          fp_gpu_jobs$mem_gb > fp_mem[[2]], ]
fp_cpu_arm <- fp_jobs[fp_jobs$job_id == det_meta("cpu", "job"), ]
stopifnot(nrow(fp_odd) > 0, all(fp_odd$category == "Diarisation probe"),
          nrow(fp_cpu_arm) == 1, fp_cpu_arm$gpus == 0,
          fp_cpu_arm$category == "Determinism check (CPU only)")
# The ledger's other jobs without a GPU, which the Methods set apart from
# the processor run (evaluation/footprint.py sets their categories), and
# none of which runs a model for a reported result. Most ran tests and
# smoke tests, probes, the sweep's aggregation or the AMI cache and its
# audit. The Methods name two kinds apart: those in the FLEURS category,
# which measured the diacritic shares the multilingual table reports
# (output/evaluation/README.md, fleurs_diacritic_shares.json), and the
# word error rate benchmark's attempts on processor cores
# (hpc/legacy/README.md), none of which completed.
fp_nogpu <- fp_jobs[fp_jobs$gpus == 0 & fp_jobs$job_id != fp_cpu_arm$job_id, ]
fp_nogpu_diac  <- fp_nogpu[fp_nogpu$category == "WER multilingual (FLEURS)", ]
fp_nogpu_pilot <- fp_nogpu[fp_nogpu$category == "WER (pilot)", ]
stopifnot(all(fp_nogpu$category %in% c(
            "Test suite and smoke tests", "Diarisation probe",
            "Aggregation (CPU only)", "AMI reconstruction (CPU only)",
            "WER multilingual (FLEURS)", "WER (pilot)")),
          nrow(fp_nogpu_diac) > 0,
          all(grepl("diac", fp_nogpu_diac$job_name)),
          nrow(fp_nogpu_pilot) > 0,
          all(startsWith(fp_nogpu_pilot$job_name, "benchmark_wer")),
          all(fp_nogpu_pilot$state != "COMPLETED"))
# "The diarisation jobs ran on NVIDIA L40S cards too": the ledger's
# diarisation jobs of the October re-run (named au_der_*), the four
# summaries' runs and the two sweeps, each held one.
fp_der <- fp_jobs[startsWith(fp_jobs$job_name, "au_der_"), ]
stopifnot(nrow(fp_der) == length(der_runs) + 2,
          all(fp_der$gpu_type == "l40s"))

# Shared theme for figures. Margins and grid lines are tuned for
# print at journal column width.
theme_paper <- function(base_size = 9) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "grey92"),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey92"),
      axis.title.x = element_text(size = base_size,
                                  margin = margin(t = 3)),
      axis.title.y = element_text(size = base_size,
                                  margin = margin(r = 3)),
      axis.text  = element_text(size = base_size - 1),
      plot.caption = element_text(size = base_size - 1, hjust = 0,
                                  margin = margin(t = 4)),
      plot.margin  = margin(2, 4, 2, 2),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.margin   = margin(t = 0, b = 0),
      legend.box.margin = margin(t = -2, b = -2),
      legend.key.height = unit(7, "pt"),
      legend.key.width  = unit(10, "pt"),
      legend.title = element_text(size = base_size),
      legend.text  = element_text(size = base_size - 1),
      strip.text = element_text(size = base_size, face = "bold")
    )
}

# Condition ordering and grouping into a three-layer registry, used by
# the figure and the appendix table.  The list is the set of conditions
# the committed sweep scored, the production stages in the order the
# composite applies them. The check below refuses a grid whose
# conditions differ from this list, since the figures filter on it and
# would otherwise drop a condition without saying so; it is how the
# re-run's seventeenth condition, `pronoun_i_fix` (audit finding
# EWER-13), came to be listed here.
condition_order <- c(
  "raw",
  "unicode_strip", "repetition_fix", "undefined_tag",
  "filler_bracket", "contraction_fix", "common_phrase_fix",
  "whitespace_normalise", "sentence_capitalise", "pronoun_i_fix",
  "punct_space_fix",
  "pipeline_full",
  "filler_strip", "dedup_window", "punct_strip", "case_fold",
  "whisper_norm"
)
if (!setequal(unique(sweep_agg$condition), condition_order))
  stop("The sweep's conditions differ from condition_order: ",
       paste(setdiff(union(unique(sweep_agg$condition), condition_order),
                     intersect(unique(sweep_agg$condition),
                               condition_order)), collapse = ", "),
       call. = FALSE)
# The conditions whose every change the scoring normaliser removes from
# both sides, as the sweep marks them (wer_invisible, audit finding
# EWER-03), in the order above. A condition marked in some cells and not
# in others is refused. wer_invisible_as_raw says whether each of them
# scores as the raw output in every corpus and model, as the WER section
# says they do by construction.
wer_invisible_conds <- local({
  inv <- tapply(sweep_agg$wer_invisible, sweep_agg$condition, unique,
                simplify = FALSE)
  if (any(lengths(inv) != 1) || anyNA(unlist(inv)))
    stop("sweep_aggregate.csv marks a condition wer_invisible in some ",
         "cells and not in others", call. = FALSE)
  intersect(condition_order, names(inv)[unlist(inv)])
})
wer_invisible_as_raw <- local({
  key <- c("suite", "model_slug")
  inv <- sweep_agg[sweep_agg$wer_invisible, c(key, "macro_wer")]
  raw <- sweep_agg[sweep_agg$condition == "raw", c(key, "macro_wer")]
  j   <- merge(inv, raw, by = key, suffixes = c("", "_raw"))
  nrow(j) == nrow(inv) && all(abs(j$macro_wer - j$macro_wer_raw) < 1e-12)
})
condition_layer <- function(cond) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    cond == "raw"                                      ~ "Baseline",
    cond == "pipeline_full"                            ~ "Production composite",
    cond == "whisper_norm"                             ~ "Canonical reference",
    cond %in% c("filler_strip", "dedup_window",
                "punct_strip", "case_fold")            ~ "Diagnostic ablation",
    TRUE                                               ~ "Production atomic"
  )
}
layer_levels <- c("Baseline", "Production atomic",
                  "Production composite", "Diagnostic ablation",
                  "Canonical reference")

suite_labels <- c(
  librispeech_clean  = "LibriSpeech clean",
  librispeech_other  = "LibriSpeech other",
  fleurs             = "FLEURS (read en)",
  voxpopuli_accented = "VoxPopuli accented",
  ami                = "AMI (meetings)"
)
```

```{r keywords-pdf, results='asis'}
# The PDF prints the keywords beneath the abstract, as Behavior Research
# Methods asks; the HTML title block prints them already. They are read
# from the front matter, as the claims check reads the abstract, so the
# two outputs cannot list different keywords.
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  kw_src <- knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)
  if (is.null(kw_src) || !file.exists(kw_src)) kw_src <- "manuscript.qmd"
  kw <- unlist(rmarkdown::yaml_front_matter(kw_src)$keywords)
  stopifnot(length(kw) > 0, all(nzchar(kw)))
  cat("\\indent\\textit{Keywords:} ", paste(kw, collapse = ", "),
      "\n\n\\clearpage\n\n",
      sep = "")
}
```

# Introduction

Recordings of speech occupy a peculiar place in the data ecology of
the social sciences. They are among the richest sources of evidence
available to a researcher and among the most legally and ethically
constrained. A single hour of interview audio may contain clinically
relevant disclosures, identifying information about third parties who
never consented to take part, and the unguarded asides on which
qualitative analysis depends, all entangled with the substantive
content of the conversation. Modern automatic speech recognition (ASR)
systems can transcribe such material in near real time
[@radford2022whisper].

Cloud transcription services, however, operate under terms of use that
can be difficult to reconcile with the data-sovereignty requirements of
human-subjects research. Where an institution acts as a data
controller, the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation
requires it to demonstrate compliance
[@generalDataProtectionRegulation2016], and in the United Kingdom the
Data Protection Act 2018 supplements the UK General Data Protection
Regulation [@dataProtectionAct2018]. Other regimes differ in scope, as
the California Consumer Privacy Act applies to covered businesses
[@californiaConsumerPrivacyAct2018] and Brazil's General Data
Protection Law exempts exclusively academic processing from all but
its provisions on lawful processing and sensitive data
[@leiGeralProtecaoDados2018]. An external transcription service raises
questions about the provider's role and about the safeguards governing
access to the recording. Cloud-hosted chatbot interfaces compound the
problem with practical limits, including caps on uploaded file size
that exclude long interviews, and opacity about model versions and
post-processing that prevents downstream reproducibility. The
practical question for the researcher is how to use ASR without losing
custody of the recording.

The workflow described here addresses that question. It packages
OpenAI's Whisper Large v3, a later model of a family first trained on
roughly 680,000 hours of weakly supervised multilingual audio
[@radford2022whisper], with optional speaker diarisation (the
attribution of each stretch of speech to a speaker) and a
post-processing layer. It runs on a researcher's own machine or on an
institutional high-performance computing cluster, and neither the
audio nor the transcript leaves the institution.

The recogniser estimates text from acoustic input through a learned
sequence model [@radford2022whisper], whose training objective does
not guarantee that every emitted word was spoken. Whisper hallucinates
plausible continuations during silence, tidies away disfluencies that
a careful researcher may wish to study, and regularises proper nouns
into more familiar near-neighbours. The first of those failure modes
has been audited from outside. @koeneckeCarelessWhisperSpeechtoText2024
found that 1.4% of the transcriptions the hosted Whisper interface
returned for 13,140 English segments, drawn from a corpus of aphasic
and control speech, contained phrases absent from the audio. The
duration of non-vocal audio in a segment was the strongest predictor of
that fabrication. That audit tested the application programming
interface as it stood in 2023 and found nothing comparable from five
competing services on the same segments. Its figure therefore
describes one system at one date and need not hold for the local model
used here. A responsible transcription pipeline includes a defensive
layer that notices these typical failure modes and either corrects
them or, where correction is unsafe, makes them visible to the analyst.

Describing such a workflow is not the same as showing that it works,
and the question this paper asks is what a defensive layer of that kind
can and cannot be shown to do. The workflow is therefore treated as an
object of measurement and put to five tests it could fail.

The first three tests concern the layer. The first asks whether it
costs accuracy. On English it did, a little, and the whole of that cost
turned out to be one defective stage. With that stage repaired and
further corrections made, the layer costs nothing on any of the
`r num_word(n_sweep_suites)` English corpora tested, though the
evidence differs between them. On its own, a null in aggregate word
error rate (WER) cannot show the stages to be harmless, because the
variation between utterances that dominates a corpus average exceeds
differences this small. Comparing the same utterances with and without
each stage cancels that variation. That paired test is reported for
Whisper Large v3 on LibriSpeech test-clean, where it finds no
difference. On the other four corpora, the claim rests on corpus
averages, which the layer nowhere raises above those of the raw
output. No null, paired or not, would show the layer's value, which
depends on the model it wraps and appears only where the decoder
fails.

The second test asks whether WER can assess the claim the layer is
offered on, that it preserves the fillers some research designs are
built from. It cannot, and scoring that property directly shows both
that the layer preserves what it receives and that the recogniser
supplies only about a fifth of them, and fewer of the hesitations
among them. The third asks whether
post-processing written against English transfers to the other
languages the workflow offers. It did not, and the failure was severe
and had gone unnoticed.

The last two tests turn from the layer to the rest of the workflow.
The fourth measures the speaker-attribution and timestamp components
on meeting speech. Scoring speaker attribution against meetings
rebuilt along their original timeline, in place of the concatenated
utterances first used, it finds that the reconstruction matters more
than any tuning decision available. The fifth asks how far the
privacy claim reaches, and finds a name masker whose behaviour is
settled by two explicit conditions, together with a voice
transformation that brings speaker linkage near chance only at the
setting that also destroys the transcript. The paper also reports how
widely error rates vary between the readers of one clean corpus,
whether repeated decodes give the same words within and across
hardware configurations, and what the evaluation cost in computation.

Alongside these results, the paper describes two complementary modes
of deployment. One is a single-command desktop application for
Windows, macOS and Linux, and the other a portable batch interface for
Slurm, the scheduler most common on academic systems. The batch
interface's submission scripts and environment-setup templates were
exercised on the University of Oxford's Advanced Research Computing
(ARC) facility and are written to run on any institutional cluster
with comparable scheduling. Between them, the two modes run the same
workflow on a researcher's own computer and on a shared cluster. The
claim attached to them concerns packaging alone, since no comparison
against an alternative local pipeline is reported here.

# Background

The failure modes sketched in the Introduction belong to a small set
that recurs across the empirical literature. Whisper and its peers are
trained on internet-mined pairs of audio and text whose alignment is
sometimes loose [@radford2022whisper], and their coverage of the
world's languages and dialects is systematically uneven
[@alumaeStrivingOpensourceEquitable2025].
@wangCalmWhisperReduceWhisper2025 showed that 3 of the 20 attention
heads in the Whisper Large v3 decoder account for the majority of
hallucinations on non-speech segments of the UrbanSound benchmark.
They also showed that a targeted fine-tuning of those heads reduces
non-speech hallucination by more than 80% at negligible cost to WER on
LibriSpeech. @zusagCrisperWhisperAccurateTimestamps2024 demonstrated
that tokeniser adjustments and verbatim fine-tuning recover the filled
pauses, false starts and self-corrections that Whisper's default
decoder regularises away, while also improving word-level timestamp
precision. @chungDiagnosisawareMultitaskFinetuning2026 reported
character-error-rate reductions of up to 18 percentage points when
Whisper was fine-tuned on Korean dysarthric speech, evidence that the
base model's failure modes are not uniformly distributed across
speaker populations.

Two recent field comparisons frame the data-sovereignty trade-off
that the present workflow addresses. @russellWhatAutomaticSpeech2024
compared six commercial and open-source systems on conversational
audio and concluded that present ASR cannot replace the trained
transcriber but can produce a defensible draft.
@landesvatterComparingSpeechtoTextAlgorithms2025 reached a
complementary conclusion on open-ended survey audio, finding the
Google Cloud service outperformed by nearly all open-source
alternatives in their sample. On this evidence, the cost of avoiding
cloud services is no longer measured straightforwardly in accuracy. An
evaluation of Whisper variants on four Raspberry Pi platforms further
established that the smaller Faster-Whisper models run with acceptable
latency on commodity single-board computers
[@caoPerformanceEvaluationWhisperSeries2025]. That result weakens the
assumption that many transcription workloads strictly require
institutional-scale infrastructure.

The closest published analogue to the present architecture is Vink,
an open-source Whisper wrapper developed and pilot-tested for
qualitative research in 14 languages and explicitly motivated by
data-protection constraints [@tolleVoiceInkVink2024]. The present
workflow adds speaker diarisation, name masking and a Slurm-managed
batch interface to that lineage. The paper's contribution lies less in
those additions than in the evaluation, which tests the
post-processing layer and the speaker-attribution, timestamp and
de-identification components against the property each is offered
for.

# Methods

This section follows a recording through the workflow, from
enhancement and recognition to post-processing, speaker attribution
and de-identification, and then sets out the protocol by which each
component was evaluated.

## Enhancement and Recognition

The pipeline accepts an audio file in any of the common formats
supported by `librosa` (WAV, MP3, M4A, FLAC, OGG, AAC). Before
transcription, the audio can pass through a fixed chain
of a constant gain, spectral subtraction with the first half second of
the recording as the noise reference, a static soft-clipping curve
applied sample by sample, and a peak normalisation applied only when
the peak would otherwise clip. The enhancement is off by default and
is intended for field recordings with steady background noise. On a
set of 74 French and English voice messages, denoising ahead of
transcription has been reported to lower WER for the smaller Whisper
models, while the unprocessed audio gave the lowest rate for the
medium, large and large-v2 models
[@trabelsiNoiseReductionImproving2024]. That finding is a reason to
leave the chain off for a model of the size used here.

The enhanced or original waveform is then passed to Whisper Large v3
through the `transformers` automatic-speech-recognition pipeline with
overlapping chunking, which bounds memory consumption on long
recordings and improves boundary behaviour at segment edges. The chunk
is 30 s long with a 5 s stride when timestamps are requested and 15 s
long with a 2 s stride when they are not, and one chunk is decoded at
a time. The model runs in half precision on a CUDA graphics processing
unit (GPU) and in single precision on a processor, and the batch
transcription jobs ask the cluster's scheduler for processor cores
alone.

When timestamps are requested, the workflow groups the model's
word-level alignment into caption-sized segments and serialises them
as a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) document and a WebVTT file.
Both are written before any post-processing, so that the timings stay
synchronised with the raw model output and downstream evaluation works
from a faithful record of what the model produced. A review pass then reads the timestamped segments and flags those whose
shape is characteristic of a decoding loop or of hallucinated filler.
It also compares the end of the final segment with the duration of the
recording, so that a transcript which stops early becomes visible. The
flags, written to a separate JSON document, are heuristic and carry no
estimate of model confidence, so they direct the analyst's attention
and decide nothing.

## Post-Processing

The post-processing layer applies 10 steps in a fixed order, two
helpers followed by eight atomic stages. The first helper, the Unicode
strip, removes emoji and the stray symbol and control characters that
surface in Whisper's output, keeping the letters, combining marks,
punctuation and numbers of every script. The second, the repetition
repair, collapses the loops Whisper occasionally produces on noisy or
silent passages, but it runs only when the user asks for it, through
the `--fix-spurious-repetitions` option.

The eight atomic stages divide into three jobs. Two make the model's
uncertainty visible. An undefined-token tagger marks the fragment
`undefined` and its variants, which appear in Whisper's output, as
`[undefined]`. A filler bracketer puts unambiguous
non-lexical fillers and hyphenated backchannels in square brackets, so
that the analyst can see them without confusing them with lexical
content. Two more act on how the decoder writes particular words. A
contraction repair restores the apostrophes the tokeniser sometimes
drops or splits off, from a table keyed on misspellings such as
`dont`. Seven of those keys were ordinary English words, a defect that
[the word error rate results](#sec-wer) take up. A common-phrase
normaliser regularises the capitalisation of a few lexical hedges,
such as *kind of* and *I mean*. The remaining four work on
orthography. A whitespace normaliser collapses runs of whitespace and
tidies the spacing around commas and full stops. A sentence capitaliser
restores the capital at the start of each sentence, in any script that
has one, and a pronoun capitaliser upper-cases the standalone English
first-person pronoun. Last, a punctuation-spacing tidier removes spaces
before punctuation and puts one after it, except between two digits, so
that decimals, thousands separators and clock times stay whole.

A language gate cuts across these three jobs. Five of the eight stages
assume an English vocabulary, the pronoun capitaliser among them, and
run only on a transcript identified as English. The other three encode
conventions many languages share and run on every transcript, for
reasons given in [the multilingual results](#sec-multilingual).

The order in which the steps are applied matters. Placeholders that
have replaced real tokens make the repetition repair brittle, so it
runs before any masking step, and the name masker runs last, on the
capitals and word boundaries the cleaning stages leave. Each atomic
stage, with its single job, is exposed at module scope and registered
as a named condition in the WER benchmark, so that its contribution
can be measured in isolation. A regression test asserts that the composite
reproduces the chained stages exactly. [Appendix A](#sec-appendix-stages)
gives each stage's formal specification and the order of application.

## Speaker Attribution and De-Identification

Speaker attribution is offered as an optional stage, built on
`pyannote.audio`. The diarisation model runs entirely on the local
machine, with model weights fetched from the Hugging Face Hub on first
use, a download that carries no user data, and served from the local
cache thereafter. Diarisation accuracy is sensitive to recording
quality and to the number and similarity of speakers, so whenever
attribution is enabled, the workflow also saves a speaker-free
transcript, which the researcher can fall back on if the diarisation
output proves unusable.

Two de-identification stages are offered on top of that. The first
masks personal names by matching the transcript against a curated list
of given names and surnames covering nine languages, with the
possessive clitic stripped before lookup so that *Anna's* is
recognised where *Anna* is, and replacing each match with a
placeholder. The detector requires an initial capital, judged on the
name itself even behind an opening quotation mark or bracket. That
keeps it from redacting the lower-case ordinary words that many names
coincide with, though not a capitalised word that names something
other than a person, such as *Jordan* for the country. Both
conditions, a listed name and an initial capital, are deliberate, and
both bound what the stage can catch, as
[the masking evaluation](#sec-masking) shows. An optional second pass
adds a zero-shot named-entity model small enough to run on a processor
[@zaratianaGLiNERGeneralistModel2024]. It only proposes further
redactions and never withdraws one the dictionary made, and every
masking decision is written to a log recording which stage was
responsible.

The second de-identification stage acts on the audio, warping the
voice through the McAdams coefficient
[@patinoSpeakerAnonymisationUsing2021].
[The voice anonymisation results](#sec-anonymisation) report what it
does to speaker linkage and to the transcript.

## Evaluation Protocol

The protocol below sets out how every transcript is scored, the
corpora and decoder settings behind the scores, the software and
hardware of the runs, the seeds and intervals, and the design of each
experiment.

### Scoring

The measure reported is WER, the proportion of reference words that a transcript
substitutes, deletes or inserts. The `evaluation.wer` module computes
it with `jiwer` against a reference corpus. The match error rate, word
information lost and character error rate are computed alongside it
and written to the committed aggregate, `sweep_aggregate.csv`, which
also holds the macro-averaged rates tabulated in
[Appendix B](#sec-appendix-results). Neither the text nor the appendix
reports those three measures. At the corpus level, the Results report
both the macro-averaged WER, which weights every utterance equally,
and the micro-averaged WER, which weights every reference word equally
and is therefore more sensitive to long utterances. Every corpus-level
WER quoted in the Results is the macro average unless stated
otherwise, because the unit of observation in the sweep is the
utterance and every condition is scored on the same utterances, bar
one. The condition that applies the canonical Whisper normaliser to
both sides empties the reference of
`r big(n_utt("ami") - n_utt("ami", "whisper_norm"))` utterances from
the AMI Meeting Corpus, and they are then dropped. Pooled micro averages
are used where utterance length would otherwise drive the figure,
namely for the per-reader rates and the intelligibility cost of voice
anonymisation, and diarisation error rate is reported both ways.

Before scoring, both sides pass through the same scoring normaliser,
`normalise_text` in `evaluation/wer.py`. It first removes the metadata
header that the workflow writes at the top of every transcript, so
that filenames and timestamps cannot influence the score. It then
deletes diarisation speaker tags, in the bracketed and bare forms the
workflow can emit, so that speaker attribution cannot change the score
either. Finally, it applies Unicode compatibility composition
(`NFKC`), replaces the curly single quotation marks with straight
apostrophes, lower-cases, replaces with a space every character that
is neither a word character, whitespace nor an apostrophe, and
collapses runs of whitespace. The apostrophe is kept deliberately, so
that a contraction is scored as the single token it is written as and
a wrongly restored apostrophe counts as an error. A single quotation
mark written as an apostrophe is kept with it. Because both sides are
normalised, a post-processing stage that changes only case, spacing,
square brackets or punctuation other than the apostrophe cannot move
the score at all, whatever it does to the transcript.
[The word error rate results](#sec-wer) name the stages of that kind.
Filler tokens are retained by default because they carry information
in many research designs, and an opt-in flag discards them.

### Corpora and Decoding

The condition sweep extends the single-condition interface to a
matrix of post-processing choices. Because the conditions act on the
decoded text, a driver loads each audio corpus once, decodes it in a
single pass and scores every registered condition against the same
hypotheses. Each of the five corpora is identified below by its
Hugging Face dataset, configuration and split, the three strings an
independent run must match. LibriSpeech test-clean and test-other
[@panayotovLibrispeechASRCorpus2015] cover read audiobook speech from
the speakers that a reference recogniser found easier and harder to
transcribe, respectively (`librispeech_asr`, configurations `clean`
and `other`, split `test`, with `r n_utt_txt("librispeech_clean")` and
`r n_utt_txt("librispeech_other")` utterances). FLEURS (Few-shot
Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech)
[@conneauFleursFewshotLearning2023] covers read multilingual speech,
restricted here to the English-US split (`google/fleurs`,
configuration `en_us`, split `test`, `r n_utt_txt("fleurs")`
utterances). VoxPopuli [@wangVoxpopuliLargescaleMultilingual2021]
supplies accented English from European Parliament debates
(`facebook/voxpopuli`, configuration `en_accented`, split `test`, the
configuration's only split, `r n_utt_txt("voxpopuli_accented")`
utterances). AMI [@carlettaAMIMeeting2005] supplies meeting speech
recorded on individual head-mounted microphones, the most acoustically
challenging condition in the present evaluation (`edinburghcstr/ami`,
configuration `ihm`, split `test`, `r n_utt_txt("ami")` utterances).
Reference text is read from the `text` field for LibriSpeech and AMI,
`transcription` for FLEURS and `normalized_text` for VoxPopuli.

The decoder used for the WER work is not the chunked configuration the
desktop workflow uses. The benchmark driver calls the same
`transformers` automatic-speech-recognition pipeline with
`return_timestamps=True`, which engages Whisper's own long-form
mechanism and leaves the chunked path unused. It passes
`language="english"` and `task="transcribe"` as generation arguments,
so that the decoder is never left to guess the language, and the
multilingual wave differs only in the value of `language`. No beam
width, sampling flag, temperature or temperature-fallback schedule is
supplied, so decoding is greedy. With no batch size set either, the
model transcribes one utterance at a time, on the first visible CUDA
device where there is one and on the processor otherwise. On a GPU,
the pipeline is given no precision and loads each checkpoint in the
precision it is stored in. Whisper Large v3 and Distil-Large v3
therefore decode in `r wer_precision` and Whisper Medium in single
precision, as the sweep's summaries record, although only the headline
cell's summary is committed. Every decode of the sweep and of the
multilingual wave ran on a GPU. Two benchmarks depart from this
configuration. The timestamp benchmark needs segment boundaries and
therefore decodes in `r ts_summary$whisper$chunk_length_s` s chunks
with a `r ts_summary$whisper$stride_length_s` s stride, while the
voice anonymisation benchmark transcribes short single-utterance clips
without chunking. Both decode in `r ts_precision` on the GPU, as
Whisper Large v3 does in the sweep, but neither forces a language, so
their transcripts are not interchangeable with the sweep's.

### Software, Hardware and Provenance

The floors that `requirements.txt` sets on the packages the code needs
include `transformers[torch]` at `r req_floor("transformers[torch]")`,
`torch` at `r req_floor("torch")`,
`pyannote.audio` at `r req_floor("pyannote.audio")`, `jiwer` at
`r req_floor("jiwer")` and `datasets` at `r req_floor("datasets")`.
The floor on `transformers` is binding, because the language gate in
the post-processing layer calls `detect_language`, which earlier
releases do not expose. A floor does not fix an environment, so the
versions installed in the cluster environment the result jobs run in
are recorded separately, in a lock taken on `r lock_taken_txt`
(`requirements-lock.txt`). Among them are `torch`
`r lock_version("torch")`,
`transformers` `r lock_version("transformers")`, `pyannote.audio`
`r lock_version("pyannote.audio")`, `jiwer` `r lock_version("jiwer")`
and `datasets` `r lock_version("datasets")`. Jobs run after the lock
was taken record in their outputs the package versions installed when
they ran. They include the jobs behind the condition sweep, the
diarisation, timestamp and voice anonymisation benchmarks, the last of
the multilingual passes and the audit of the reconstructed AMI
meetings. The records committed from the sweep's headline cell, the
diarisation, timestamp and anonymisation benchmarks and the audit match
the lock package for package. For jobs run before it, the lock
describes the environment only as it stood when it was taken and
cannot by itself show that nothing in it changed from one job to the
next.

A preflight module aborts a job when a floor is unmet or, for a GPU
job, when no CUDA device is visible. It ran at the head of the jobs
behind the condition sweep, the diarisation, timestamp and
anonymisation benchmarks, the determinism check and the last of the
multilingual passes. The first
`r num_word(length(ml$benchmark$arms) - 1)` multilingual passes, which
predate it, ran without it. In the diarisation jobs, it also required
that `pyannote.audio` import and its gated model be available. The
condition sweep's aggregate records the code the sweep ran,
`r sweep_version`, and the diarisation summaries record the code of
their runs, `r der_commit`, together with the package versions,
`pyannote.audio` `r der_summary$pyannote_audio_version` among them.

The manuscript is a Quarto document. Its figures, tables and quoted
results are generated at render time from the committed JSON and
comma-separated values (CSV) artefacts the evaluation modules produce,
except where the text names another source. A regenerated artefact
therefore changes the reported numbers without any being retyped, and
a missing or malformed one stops the render, so that no older figure
survives in its place. Release `r cff$version` of the workflow
[@bernabeuSecureScalableSpeech2026] archives the code, run records and
committed results behind the manuscript, whereas its first release,
1.0.0 [@bernabeuSecureScalableSpeech2025], predates the evaluation
modules and produced none of the results reported here. The full test suite,
the Slurm submission scripts and the post-processing implementation
are catalogued in the repository linked at the end of the paper.

The jobs behind the reported results ran in the `short` partition of
the htc cluster at the University of Oxford. The committed scheduler
ledger, captured on `r long_date(fp$provenance$captured)` after the
last job of the main evaluation had finished, records each job's
allocation and, read from the node it ran on, the board of every GPU,
`r num_word(fp_n_boards)` models in all. Each GPU job held one GPU
and, apart from `r num_word(nrow(fp_odd))` diarisation probes,
`r num_word(fp_cores[[1]])` to `r num_word(fp_cores[[2]])` processor
cores and `r fp_mem[[1]]` to `r fp_mem[[2]]` GB of memory, as its
submission script requests. Of the jobs that ran a model for a
reported result, the determinism check's processor run alone held no
GPU, with `r num_word(fp_cpu_arm$cpus)` cores and
`r fp_cpu_arm$mem_gb` GB. The ledger's `r num_word(nrow(fp_nogpu))`
other jobs without a GPU ran tests, probes, aggregation or the
preparation and checks of the data. The exceptions are
`r num_word(nrow(fp_nogpu_diac))` that measured the share of FLEURS
reference words carrying a diacritic, for the multilingual results,
and `r num_word(nrow(fp_nogpu_pilot))` attempts to run the WER
benchmark on processor cores, none of which completed.

The condition sweep decoded Whisper Large v3 on
`r wer_summary$benchmark$decode$gpu` cards, the card the summary
behind the headline figures names, and the other two models on NVIDIA
L40S cards, as `hpc/runs/sweep.env` records job by job. The timestamp
benchmark ran on an `r ts_summary$whisper$gpu`, as its summary
records. The voice anonymisation benchmark ran on an NVIDIA L40S,
which `hpc/runs/anonymisation.env` names because the benchmark's
summary does not. The diarisation jobs ran on NVIDIA L40S cards too,
which their records under `hpc/runs/` name for the same reason.
The last multilingual pass spread its languages over NVIDIA
`r and_list(ml_last_cards)` cards, named language by language in its
summary.

The determinism check transcribes the first `r big(det_n)` AMI test
utterances, all from meeting `r det_meetings`, twice under one seed and
again under a second, on each of `r num_word(det_n_own_cards)` cards
and on a processor. It ran first on an `r det_gpu_name` and writes the
card into its own output, because the same seed on a different
accelerator is a different experiment. It was repeated on an
`r det_card_names[["l40s"]]`, on an `r det_cpu_name` processor with no
GPU at all, and on a `r det_card_names[["v100_seed0"]]` in the node
that had held the condition sweep's own decode of the same utterances.
The same model's transcripts of those utterances, the sweep's among
them, can therefore be compared across `r num_word(det_n_runs)` runs
in `r num_word(det_n_configs)` hardware configurations, each a card
with the node that holds it or, for the processor run, the node alone.
The `r num_word(length(det_cards))` runs on a GPU decoded in
`r det_precision` and the processor run in `r det_cpu_precision`, as
the workflow does on a machine without a CUDA device, and the runs
also differ in seed, code and process.

The check's first `r num_word(det_n_own_before_lock)` runs predate
the lock, but other evidence shows that its environment did not change
from one run to the next. The preflight lines of its logs and the
environment records of the sweep's run and of the check's
`r num_word(det_n_own_after_lock)` runs made after the lock all name
the same versions. The preflight of its processor run found all
`r big(length(lock_pins))` pins of the lock matched, and no package
installed in the environment is newer than the earliest of its runs
(`determinism_cross_accelerator.json`).
[The reproducibility results](#sec-determinism) report what the check
found.

### Seeds, Intervals and Sensitivity Analyses

Seeds are fixed and recorded. The sweep passes `--seed 42`, which
seeds Python, NumPy and PyTorch, requests deterministic cuDNN kernels
and sets `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG` before the CUDA context is created.
The seed is written into every summary the run produces, and the
masking benchmark draws its names under the same seed. The bootstrap
fixes its seed at module scope in `evaluation/bootstrap_ci.py`, from
which `evaluation/condition_ci.py` imports it, so any interval in this
paper can be recomputed from the committed per-utterance reports
without decoding anything again. Intervals are drawn with
`r boot_b_txt` replicates, above the module default of
